newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Environmentalists call for biosafety rules.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists call for biosafety rules.

text.p: Environmentalists on Tuesday called for a moratorium on the production of genetically altered foods until nations sign a planned protocol on biosafety.
"There are serious doubts about the long-term health and ecological effects of genetically engineered organisms," Arnaud Apoteker, chief biodiversity expert for Greenpeace in France, told reporters.

"We must stop their release, because at the rate we our going our children may never eat 'natural' foods. Like with mad cow disease, the first health problems may be years away and there will be no turning back," he said.
Greenpeace focused its campaign on soybeans made by the U.S. firm Monsanto Co.. These seeds, modified to resist a strong herbicide, are sown in the United States and Argentina.
Apoteker was in Buenos Aires to take part in a biosafety workshop held parallel to the Second Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biodiversity.

The conference, which runs until Nov. 15 to discuss issues related to the protection of natural resources, will bring under review the progress of a special working group on biosafety which met recently in Denmark. The group must produce a protocol by 1998, but critics said that is too late.

"When these organisms are released into the environment they multiply, you cannot get rid of them. And if there are health problems it may be impossible to trace their origin, because by then there will be so many altered genes," said Apoteker.
"Soybeans are just the beginning of a radical change in the human food chain and ecosystems," said Apoteker.
Monsanto's beans were the first gene-altered product to be approved by the European Union for human consumption.

But consumer groups and leading food companies in countries like France, Sweden and Germany are already voicing their concerns over the altered beans. Greenpeace prepared on Tuesday to picket the arrival of the first Monsanto shipment in Hamburg.
An estimated two percent of the present U.S. harvest and four percent of Argentina's net harvest are Monsanto beans.

The Biodiversity Convention's future biosafety protocol aims to regulate the transport, use and trade of gene-modified organisms. "It's in the early stages, and there have already been strong clashes," said Apoteker. "Meanwhile many countries are serving as the playground for multinational companies to test their products."
